title: Your first gradient
summary: Find how sensitive a calculation is to each input.
description: Square two numbers and add them. A gradient measures how the result responds to each input; here it is twice that input. Change [-1, 2] and run again.

python.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(
    [-1.0, 2.0],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)

loss = (x * x).sum()
loss.backward()

print(x.grad.tolist())  # [-2.0, 4.0]

diagram.explanation: The gradient is twice each original input.

title: A weighted sum
summary: Give inputs different weights and see their effect on the result.
description: Give [1, 2] weights of [3, 4] to get 11. Change the weights and compare the result and its input gradients.

python.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(
    [1., 2.],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)
weights = torch.tensor([3., 4.], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)

loss = (x * weights).sum()
(gradient,) = torch.autograd.grad(loss, (x,))

print("loss:", loss.tolist())
print("gradient:", gradient.tolist())

diagram.explanation: Each weight measures the effect of its input on the total.

title: Two input gradients
summary: Explore how two sets of inputs influence the same result.
description: Compare how x and y affect the same result. The Python version checks the original values; update its assertions if you change those inputs.

python.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(
    [2.0, 3.0],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)
y = torch.tensor(
    [5.0, 7.0],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)

loss = (x * y + x * x).sum()
dx, dy = torch.autograd.grad(loss, (x, y))

assert dx.tolist() == [9.0, 13.0]
assert dy.tolist() == [2.0, 3.0]
assert not dx.requires_grad

print("dx:", dx.tolist())
print("dy:", dy.tolist())

diagram.explanation: Both inputs influence the same scalar result.

title: Multiply matrices
summary: Multiply two tables of numbers, then explore how their inputs affect the result.
description: Multiply a 2×3 matrix by a 3×2 matrix. Each value in seed weights one output; the input gradients measure how their weighted sum changes. Changing seed changes the gradients, not the product. Update the Python assertions if you change its inputs.

python.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor(
    [[1., 2., 3.], [4., 5., 6.]],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)
b = torch.tensor(
    [[7., 8.], [9., 10.], [11., 12.]],
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device=device,
    requires_grad=True,
)

y = a @ b
assert y.tolist() == [[58., 64.], [139., 154.]]

seed = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
ga, gb = torch.autograd.grad(y, (a, b), grad_outputs=seed)
assert ga.tolist() == [[23., 29., 35.], [53., 67., 81.]]
assert gb.tolist() == [[13., 18.], [17., 24.], [21., 30.]]

print("product:", y.tolist())
print("dA:", ga.tolist())
print("dB:", gb.tolist())

diagram.explanation: The inner dimensions match; the outer dimensions shape the result. The seed weights the gradients, not this product.
